notes.general_comments: The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all of the questions. The paper discriminated successfully between candidates of different abilities but was accessible to all. The paper was generally well answered, with very few unanswered questions . In Question 1 , most candidates obtained results that were comparable with those expected. In Question 2 , when reagents are added to a solution in a test - tube, the components of the mixture should be combined in some way , such as by shaking. Observations describing different coloured layers suggest that some candidates do not ensure the reagents are mixed. In answering the planning question ( Question 3 ) , there is no need for candidates to spend time writing a list of variables or to write a list of apparatus at the start, or the aims of the experiment. Where there is credit available for the use of suitable apparatus, then that will only be awarded if it is stated what the apparatus is used for . Credit w ill not be awarded just for a name in a list of other apparatus.
notes.1b: Most candidates produced sensible graph scales ; the most common being each large grid square being either 4 or 5  C. Those who chose difficult scales often made errors in the plotting and so did not gain the credit available for the correct plotting of all five points. The best fit line could be either a curve or a straight line, depending on the data obtained in the experiments. Many candidates drew straight lines when the points were clearly on a curve of decreasi ng gradient, in these cases credit for the best fit line was not awarded.
notes.1c: Most candidates were able to continue their graph line to the right so that a reading could be made at 45 cm . A significant number of candidates did not include the unit (  C ) in their answer; all physical quantities should be accompanied by a unit.
notes.1d: The calculation of the energy given out was completed successfully by the majority of candidates.
notes.1e: Most candidates realised that the increased mass of anhydrous lithium chloride would result in an increased temperature change. However, to gain full credit , candidates were required to give a quantitative answer. Two different quantitative answer were accepted: • The temperature change would be double the temperature change of Experiment 1 because the mass of anhydrous lithium chloride had doubled. • The temperature change would be the same as Experiment 4 because the ratio of anhydrous lithium chloride : water was the same as in Experiment 4. Some candidates incorrectly based their explanation on more anhydrous lithium chloride requiring more energy to dissolve. As the process is exothermic, energy is released and not taken in.
notes.1f: The required answer was based on polystyrene acting as an insulator and so would reduce heat loss from the solution. Less heat energy lost would mean a larger temperature rise. A significant number of candidates based their answer on the polystyrene cup being a more accurate method of measuring a volume than a beaker.
notes.1gi: The vast majority of candidates correctly stated that a burette measures volumes more accurately than a measuring cylinder.
notes.1gii: This proved to be a demanding question. In the experiments , heat energy is given out and results in the temperature of the solution increasing. Heat energy lost from the system (the beaker) results in a smaller temperature increase. If the beaker is stood in a water - bath , then more heat energy will be transferred from the beaker to the water - bath and so the temperature change will be even smaller, or possibly so small so as to be not measurable with the apparatus provided. Water - baths maintain a constant temperature and so are not suitable when the dependent variab le (the required outcome of the investigation) is the temperature change.
notes.2a: Most candidates correctly reported the formation of a green precipitate on the dropwise addition of aqueous sodium hydroxide. That precipitate should have remained when excess aqueous sodium hydroxide was added, although a number of candidates stated that the precipitate then dissolved; this is not possible.
notes.2b: The instructions tell candidates to add the sample of aqueous chlorine followed by the starch solution. The order of addition is important . It was clear that some candidates added the starch and then the chlorine. Addition of aqueous chlorine will result in the oxidation of iodide ions to iodine. This should have resulted in aqueous iodine, giving the solution a yellow, orange or brown colour. A ddition of starch would then cause the formation of a blue - black precipitate. The observations were therefore a description of the colour changes. Candidates who did not follow the order of addition in the question would have missed the initial colour of the aqueous iodine formed.
notes.2c: This was the test for halide ions. As solid J contained iodide ions, a yellow precipitate was expected. Although some candidates stated that there was no change, most noted the formation of a precipitate. The identification of the colour of the precipitate is difficult but it is expected that candida tes will be familiar with the qualitative test for halide ions and to be aware of the difficulty.
notes.2d: Most candidates correctly noted the formation of a precipitate. This precipitate should have been green or grey - green. Some candidates also noted the very small amount of effervescence that occurs as the carbonate ions react with the low concentration of h ydrogen ions present in the solution.
notes.2e: Almost all candidates who had given correct observations then correctly identified solid J as iron( II ) iodide. The oxidation state of the iron was required.
notes.2f: Candidates who performed well on Question 2 overall almost always reported the formation of a lilac flame. If the centre supervisor reported a different colour, then candidates were awarded credit for stating the same colour as the supervisor even if that colour was not lilac ; this allows for a centre having a contaminated sample. Almost all supervisors reported the formation of a lilac flame.
notes.2gi: As the salt did not contain ammonium ions, there would not have been any ammonia formed and so the red litmus paper should not have changed. A common incorrect answer was to state that the red litmus paper became blue, this is either because that is what m any candidates expect red litmus to do or because rather than holding the red litmus paper above the boiling tube they pushed it into the boiling tube and it touched the side s which had traces of aqueous sodium hydroxide on them .
notes.2gii: Candidates who performed well on Question 2 overall often correctly stated that either solid K was not an ammonium salt or that no ammonia had been made. A common incorrect answer was to say that an acid was made or that solid K was acidic ; red litmus not changing does not show an acid has been made as red litmus can detect alkalis but not acids ; blue litmus can detect acids but not alkalis.
notes.2giii: As the instructions say ‘ T est any gas given off ’ candidates were expected to report a positive test and result for a gas. As two marks were available, that means there must be another mark for an observation other than the positive gas test. The test conducted was the test for nitrate ions. Hence candid ates were expected to test for ammonia gas using damp red litmus paper, which would have become blue. The expected other observation was that there was bubbling or fizzing of effervescence in the react ion mixture.
notes.2h: While many candidates correctly identified solid K as potassium nitrate, it was not uncommon for candidates to ignore their flame test result from 2(f) .
